_产业链总览: The entire AI industry chain can be roughly divided into three stages: (1) Upstream = the hardware and infrastructure that build 'compute' (chips, equipment, data centers, power), akin to building factories and making engines; (2) Midstream = using compute to 'forge' the AI brain (large models) and supporting software; (3) Downstream = putting the AI brain to work and turning it into products that make money (coding, office work, autonomous driving, robotics, etc.). The further upstream, the higher the certainty (the shovel sellers); the further downstream, the greater the imagination but the more undecided the outcome.

nodes.name: AI Compute Chips
nodes.desc: The GPUs / accelerators used to train and run large models — the most certain 'shovel seller' of this AI wave.

explainer.what: The reason AI is 'smart' comes down to enormous amounts of math, and the supercomputing chips built specifically for this work are AI compute chips (mainly GPUs). Think of them as the 'engine' in the AI factory — whether training a model or having the model answer your questions (called inference), it all comes down to this chip doing the math.
explainer.position: The most upstream and most core link of the entire chain. Its capacity and performance directly determine how powerful the AI built downstream can be. Right now NVIDIA holds a near-monopoly and is the industry's acknowledged 'shovel seller' (the one selling shovels in a gold rush profits no matter who strikes gold).
explainer.watch: The highest certainty and the most direct beneficiary of AI spending. Watch three things: whether NVIDIA's dominance gets eroded by cloud providers' in-house chips and AMD, export controls on advanced chips to China, and whether downstream demand overheats and pulls forward future orders.

nodes.name: Cloud Providers' In-House Chips
nodes.desc: AI chips designed in-house by cloud providers to reduce reliance on NVIDIA, such as Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, and Huawei Ascend.

explainer.what: Big cloud providers like Google and Amazon spend tens of billions of dollars a year buying chips from NVIDIA — expensive and dependent on others — so they simply design their own chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Huawei Ascend). It's like a major customer, tired of an overbearing supplier, building its own engine.
explainer.position: Sits at the same upstream position as AI compute chips above, and is NVIDIA's 'internal competitor.' The more successful these giants' in-house efforts, the weaker NVIDIA's pricing power.
explainer.watch: Watch how much share these in-house chips can take from NVIDIA. The real beneficiaries are often not the cloud providers themselves but the likes of Broadcom and TSMC that help them with chip design and foundry work.

nodes.name: Wafer Foundry
nodes.desc: The foundries that turn chip designs into physical products; advanced-process capacity is a hard bottleneck for AI chips.

explainer.what: Chip companies like NVIDIA actually only draw the blueprints and don't run factories themselves; the ones that truly turn the blueprints into physical chips are the foundries. Like an architect drawing plans and a construction crew building the tower, TSMC is the world's best 'chip construction crew.'
explainer.position: The step right after chip design and the gateway all AI chips must pass through. The most advanced processes can essentially only be made by TSMC, making it a hard bottleneck for the whole chain.
explainer.watch: Advanced-process (2nm/3nm) capacity is a scarce resource — only those who get in line get supply. TSMC is a shared lifeline for both NVIDIA and Apple; China being locked out of advanced processes is a long-term variable.

nodes.name: Semiconductor Equipment
nodes.desc: The lithography, etching, deposition and other equipment used to make chips — 'the shovel seller's shovel seller.'

explainer.what: To make chips, foundries first have to spend big money buying a pile of extremely precise machines — lithography systems, etchers, deposition equipment, and so on. The companies selling these machines are 'the shovel seller's shovel seller' (selling mining machines to the gold diggers).
explainer.position: Even further upstream than the foundries. Without ASML's lithography systems from the Netherlands, TSMC couldn't even make advanced chips, so it sits at the very source of the entire chain.
explainer.watch: ASML's EUV lithography systems are the world's sole supply and hugely sought after. China can't buy high-end equipment, so domestic substitution (Naura, AMEC, etc.) is a certain long-term theme.

nodes.name: Semiconductor Materials
nodes.desc: Consumables for chip manufacturing such as silicon wafers, photoresist and specialty gases — they benefit alongside capacity expansion.

explainer.what: Making chips is like cooking: besides the machines (equipment), you also need ingredients and seasonings — consumables like silicon wafers, photoresist and specialty gases. Each chip made consumes a batch, and once used up you have to keep buying more.
explainer.position: The upstream consumables link, hidden behind equipment and foundries. It ramps up along with chip capacity expansion, but its unit price is low and its presence is faint.
explainer.watch: Many high-end materials are monopolized by Japanese firms, another potential chokepoint. There is room for domestic substitution, but the stock-price elasticity is usually not as strong as in the equipment segment.

nodes.name: Advanced Packaging (CoWoS)
nodes.desc: Packaging GPUs and HBM together at high density (CoWoS, etc.) — another major bottleneck for compute-chip capacity.

explainer.what: An AI chip is actually a 'composite' that tightly assembles the computing core together with several high-speed memory chips (HBM). CoWoS is the advanced packaging process that completes this high-difficulty assembly.
explainer.position: The back-end step right after wafer foundry, and another major bottleneck for AI chip mass production — if CoWoS capacity is short, NVIDIA can't ship even if the chips are made.
explainer.watch: CoWoS has been in long-term short supply and is seen as a direct 'valve' on NVIDIA's shipment volume. It is currently led by TSMC, and related packaging-and-test houses benefit as they expand capacity.

nodes.name: HBM / Memory
nodes.desc: The high-bandwidth memory (HBM) next to AI chips — a new memory battleground with exploding demand.

explainer.what: AI chips compute at lightning speed, but they need memory fast enough to feed them data, or the engine spins in vain no matter how strong it is. This ultra-high-speed memory tucked right next to the GPU is HBM. Regular memory is like a distant warehouse; HBM is like a high-speed rack at your side.
explainer.position: A core upstream complement, shipped bundled with the GPU, with demand riding the AI boom. It is one of the few links that can be as tight as GPUs themselves.
explainer.watch: Monopolized by three players — SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung — with technology iterating to HBM3E/HBM4. When supply is tight, pricing power is very strong, making it the most elastic sub-segment of the memory industry.

nodes.name: Optical Modules / Optical Interconnect
nodes.desc: The 'highway' that moves data between GPUs inside data centers; demand for 800G/1.6T optical modules surges with compute.

explainer.what: An AI data center holds tens of thousands of GPUs that must work together to compute a single large model, so they need to exchange data with each other at ultra-high speed. Optical modules are the 'fiber-optic highway tollbooths' connecting these GPUs, responsible for converting electrical signals into light and back again.
explainer.position: The upstream 'interconnect' link inside data centers. The greater the compute and the more GPUs stacked, the more optical modules are needed — a classic 'rising tide lifts all boats.'
explainer.watch: Speeds upgrade every year or two (400G→800G→1.6T), driving continuous replacement demand. Chinese makers (Zhongji Innolight, Eoptolink) lead globally and are one of the A-share AI themes.

nodes.name: Servers / Data Centers
nodes.desc: Assembling chips into AI servers and data center racks — the link that rides the 'construction boom.'

explainer.what: Chips alone can't be used; you have to assemble the chips, memory, power supplies, network cards and so on into AI servers, then stack them into racks and fill entire data center buildings. This is the 'assembly + building' link.
explainer.position: The mid-to-late part of upstream, integrating all the components above into compute infrastructure that can actually run, riding the dividends of the AI 'construction boom.'
explainer.watch: High volume but low gross margin — more like 'selling labor.' Assembly leaders such as Supermicro, Foxconn Industrial Internet and Dell are representative; orders and capex are the barometers of the cycle.

nodes.name: Cloud Compute / Rental
nodes.desc: Cloud providers and GPU rental firms that lease out compute — the 'utility companies' of the AI era.

explainer.what: The vast majority of companies can neither afford nor fully use thousands of GPUs, so cloud providers rent out compute by the hour — pay for what you use. This is the 'utility company' of the AI era: it doesn't sell generators, it sells electricity.
explainer.position: Standing at the 'exit' of upstream infrastructure, directly serving everyone downstream who wants to use AI — the hub between hardware and applications.
explainer.watch: The three giants Amazon / Microsoft / Google, plus newcomers like CoreWeave that specialize in GPU rental. Their quarterly capex is one of the most important indicators for gauging the overall AI cycle.

nodes.name: Power / Energy / Nuclear
nodes.desc: Surging data center power use is boosting power equipment, the grid and nuclear power (including small modular reactors, SMRs).

explainer.what: Data centers are outright 'power hogs' — once AI takes off, there isn't enough electricity. So the power equipment, grid and even nuclear power that supply data centers get swept up too. A GW-scale data center's power draw can rival a small city's.
explainer.position: The upstream of the upstream — supplying energy to the entire compute chain. Once the most overlooked, it has now become an increasingly hard ceiling: without power, no amount of chips can even boot up.
explainer.watch: Power is tight for U.S. data centers, and restarting nuclear plants and betting on small modular reactors (SMRs) have become the new story. Rising electricity prices also spark pushback from residents and regulators — a political risk point for AI expansion.

nodes.name: Liquid Cooling
nodes.desc: Cooling solutions for high-power AI chips; rising rack power density is rapidly boosting liquid-cooling adoption.

explainer.what: AI chips run at extremely high power and generate staggering heat — fans alone can no longer keep up, so liquid is used to touch the chip directly and carry the heat away. It's like upgrading a feverish server from an 'electric fan' to 'water-cooled air conditioning.'
explainer.position: A supporting link for upstream data centers. The denser the chips packed into a rack and the higher the power, the more liquid cooling becomes a necessity.
explainer.watch: Rapidly rising liquid-cooling adoption is a fairly high-certainty trend, with Envicool, Vertiv and others as the main beneficiaries.

nodes.name: Closed-Source Large Models
nodes.desc: Closed frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others, monetized through subscriptions and API calls.

explainer.what: Companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google spend tens to hundreds of billions of dollars and massive compute to 'forge' the strongest AI brains, but they don't reveal the internal workings — you only get to use them by paying via subscription or per API call. It's like a Michelin restaurant: the recipe is secret, they only sell the finished dish.
explainer.position: The core of the midstream — turning upstream compute into real 'intelligence.' This is the most cash-burning and most contested link of the whole chain.
explainer.watch: They stay ahead by continuously burning cash, and their profitability has always been questioned. The key points: whose model is strongest, how safety and regulation are handled, and whether they can hold their pricing power (being forced to cut prices by open-source models would hurt).

nodes.name: Open-Source / Domestic Models
nodes.desc: The open-weight and Chinese large-model camp: Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi and others.

explainer.what: The opposite of closed-source, these models publish the 'recipe' (model weights) so anyone can download them for free to deploy and modify themselves. Representatives include Meta's Llama, as well as China's DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi and others.
explainer.position: Midstream, the challenger to closed-source large models. It sharply lowers the barrier and cost of using AI, letting small and mid-size companies and individuals run models locally.
explainer.watch: China's open-source models offer high value for money and are catching up fast — the biggest highlight of this line. A counterintuitive logic: if closed-source vendors tighten restrictions too much, they instead push customers toward open-source.

nodes.name: Data / Annotation
nodes.desc: The collection, cleaning, annotation and synthesis of data needed for model training.

explainer.what: For AI to get smart, someone first has to collect massive amounts of data, clean it up, label it and feed it in — like preparing textbooks and answer keys for a student. This is the data and annotation link.
explainer.position: The 'raw material supply' link of the midstream, serving model training. No matter how strong a model is, it first has to consume enough good data.
explainer.watch: High-quality data on the internet is nearly used up and increasingly scarce; using AI to generate its own training data (synthetic data) is a new direction.

nodes.name: Frameworks / Toolchains
nodes.desc: Training/inference frameworks and development toolchains: PyTorch, CUDA, vector databases, MLOps and more.

explainer.what: The various software tools and 'scaffolding' developers use to train and deploy AI models, such as PyTorch, NVIDIA's CUDA, and vector databases. Like the scaffolding and toolbox you can't build a tower without.
explainer.position: The low-level software layer of the midstream, connecting hardware (chips) and the models above — an invisible but critical hub.
explainer.watch: NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem is its true invisible moat — once people get used to it, they can't leave. Vector databases and inference frameworks are emerging startup opportunities.

nodes.name: AI Agents
nodes.desc: Agents that can autonomously complete multi-step tasks — seen as the next stop for large-model applications.

explainer.what: Not just chatting one question at a time, but an 'AI employee' that can break a task into multiple steps on its own, call various tools, and get the job done step by step. For example, you say 'book me the cheapest flight to Shanghai next week and email it to me,' and it handles the whole thing automatically.
explainer.position: The downstream application layer, widely seen as the next big wind for large models to land and monetize.
explainer.watch: The imagination is huge, but it's still early. The core challenge is 'whether it can reliably and consistently get complex tasks right' — a high error rate means no one dares truly rely on it.

nodes.name: AI Coding
nodes.desc: AI coding assistants (Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, etc.) — currently one of the most commercially successful AI applications.

explainer.what: AI tools that help programmers — and even people who can't code — write code (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, etc.). You describe what you need in plain language, and it directly generates a runnable program.
explainer.position: One of the most profitable and most successfully deployed directions in the downstream application layer, already generating real revenue and changing how the software industry works.
explainer.watch: It is directly disrupting traditional software companies (the market calls it the SaaSpocalypse, with software stocks losing hundreds of billions in market cap overnight). Anthropic and others reach profitability precisely on this business.

nodes.name: Enterprise Software / SaaS
nodes.desc: Embedding AI capabilities into enterprise software, charged by seat or usage.

explainer.what: Putting AI capabilities into the office, customer service, CRM (customer management) and ERP software enterprises use every day, charged per user or by usage. It makes existing software smarter and more automated.
explainer.position: The downstream application layer, monetizing mainly through enterprise customers — one of the most direct battlegrounds for AI commercialization.
explainer.watch: It is both a beneficiary of AI and potentially disrupted by it — when AI can directly eliminate certain software jobs, the old per-'seat' pricing model takes a hit. Palantir is a typical example.

nodes.name: Consumer Apps
nodes.desc: AI apps for individual users such as chat, search, and image/video generation.

explainer.what: AI products ordinary people use directly — chat assistants (ChatGPT, Doubao), AI search, AI image generation and AI video generation.
explainer.position: The downstream application layer, aimed at individual consumers (To C) — the most direct entry point through which the public experiences AI.
explainer.watch: Users and traffic are huge, but monetization is hard and it easily falls into price wars and homogenized competition. Who can build a true 'super app' is the biggest suspense.

nodes.name: Autonomous Driving
nodes.desc: AI landing in cars: Robotaxi and intelligent driving solutions.

explainer.what: Letting AI drive — from assisted intelligent driving that helps you out, to fully driverless robotaxis.
explainer.position: A downstream application, AI landing in the huge automotive industry — AI in the 'physical world.'
explainer.watch: Tesla FSD and Google Waymo lead. The key is the commercialization inflection point and whether the cost per mile can drop below that of a human driver.

nodes.name: Humanoid Robots / Embodied AI
nodes.desc: Humanoid robots and embodied intelligence — AI moving from the digital world into the physical world.

explainer.what: Giving AI a body so it can do physical work in the real world, such as humanoid robots. AI thus steps out of the screen into the physical world — this is called 'embodied intelligence.'
explainer.position: A downstream application and one of the most long-term imaginative directions, seen as one of AI's 'ultimate forms.'
explainer.watch: Tesla Optimus and various startups are piling in. But it's still very early before mass production and truly useful work, and for now there's a lot of thematic hype.

nodes.name: AI Hardware
nodes.desc: On-device hardware such as AI phones / PCs / glasses and their supply chains.

explainer.what: Putting AI directly into phones, computers, glasses and other wearable devices (called 'on-device AI,' no need to connect to the cloud every time), making the devices themselves smart.
explainer.position: A downstream application, the meeting point of AI and consumer electronics, and the vehicle for spreading AI into everyone's pocket.
explainer.watch: New form factors like AI glasses and AI PCs are emerging, which will drive consumer electronics supply chains such as Luxshare and Sunny Optical. The key question is whether there will be a next 'iPhone moment.'

nodes.name: Vertical Industries
nodes.desc: AI solutions and industry-specific large models for healthcare, finance, manufacturing and other verticals.

explainer.what: AI solutions and 'industry large models' tailored to a specific industry such as healthcare, finance or manufacturing. General models know a lot broadly, while industry models dig deeper into a specialized field.
explainer.position: A downstream application, representing AI's 'last mile' penetration into traditional industries.
explainer.watch: Deployment is difficult (industry data is closed and requirements are rigorous), but once done the ceiling is high. Medical AI, AI drug discovery and AI for Science are current hotspots.
